extract:
Cornelis Vreeswijk was a Dutch-born Swedish singer-songwriter, poet, and actor, born in IJmuiden in the Netherlands in 1937 and emigrating with his family to Sweden in 1949, settling eventually in the Stockholm area. He emerged in the early 1960s as one of the central figures in the Swedish visa revival, the troubadour and folk-song scene that flourished in clubs like Visans Vänner and around venues such as Vita Hästen. Active from the early 1960s until his death in 1987, he became, despite never relinquishing his Dutch citizenship, one of the most beloved and distinctly Swedish-language voices of his generation.

His formative influences were a striking blend of the Swedish visa tradition exemplified by Evert Taube and Carl Michael Bellman, the literary chanson of Georges Brassens, and American folk and blues, particularly the calypso and acoustic blues idioms he absorbed in the late 1950s. He came up alongside contemporaries like Fred Åkerström and Ann-Louise Hanson, both of whom would interpret and record his songs, and he forged a long working relationship with Åkerström in particular, the two often associated as the leading male troubadours of the Swedish folk wave.

Vreeswijk's debut album Ballader och oförskämdheter appeared in 1964 on Metronome and immediately announced his idiom: sharp social satire, tender ballads, and a streetwise sympathy for outsiders, drunks, and prostitutes, written in colloquial Swedish marked by his audible Dutch accent. Across the 1960s he developed a recurring cast of characters, most famously the small-time crook Cornelis and his friends in the Ann-Katrin and Fredrik songs, and the Blues för Victor Jara and other politically pointed material reflecting his leftist sympathies. Albums like Tio vackra visor och Personliga Person (1968) and Spring mot Ulla, spring! (1971), along with celebrated single tracks such as Brev från kolonien, Somliga går med trasiga skor and Cecilia Lind, became staples of Swedish popular culture. He also recorded an album of Brassens interpretations and dedicated work to the poet Nils Ferlin, underlining his literary ambitions.

He worked with various Swedish labels over the years, including Metronome and later Polydor and YTF, and collaborated with arrangers and musicians from the Swedish jazz and folk worlds. Critical reception was complicated: he was adored by audiences and respected by fellow songwriters, but his bohemian lifestyle, escalating alcoholism, and tax troubles produced a turbulent public image. By the late 1970s he had fallen out of fashion with parts of the press, though albums such as Bananer - bland annat from that era and his continued live presence kept him in the public eye.

Vreeswijk died in Stockholm in November 1987, but his standing has only grown since. His songs remain part of the Swedish songbook, taught in schools and covered by successive generations from Stefan Sundström to Lars Winnerbäck and Sofia Karlsson; the Cornelis Vreeswijk Sällskapet preserves his legacy, and a museum in Stockholm has been devoted to his life and work. He is now widely regarded, alongside Taube and Bellman, as one of the defining troubadours of the Swedish language.
title: Cornelis Vreeswijk
